sessions.title: Listening for Information and Following Instructions
indicators: Listen attentively and recall details from a short passage
Follow a sequence of two or three oral instructions
Ask relevant questions for clarification using polite language
Work in pairs to give and follow instructions (collaboration, communication)
Listen to digital audio recordings and respond appropriately (digital literacy)
Reflect on the importance of careful listening in daily life (personal development)
sessions.content:
Listen Well – Ears and Minds Open

Good listening means paying full attention to the speaker. You understand more, learn better and stay safe.

1. Listening for Details

When someone speaks, listen for the important points: who, what, where, when.

Example passage: 'Every morning, Adwoa wakes up at six o'clock. She brushes her teeth, eats porridge for breakfast and then walks to school with her brother Kofi. They always arrive before the bell rings.'

Questions: What time does Adwoa wake up? What does she eat? How does she go to school?

Activity 1 – Listen and draw
Your teacher will describe a simple scene: 'A small round hut with a thatched roof, a big mango tree beside it and three chickens in front.' Listen carefully and draw what you hear. Compare your drawing with a partner. (collaboration).

2. Following Instructions

Instructions must be followed in the right order. Listen for words like first, next, then, finally.

Example: 'First, take out your exercise book. Next, open to a blank page. Then write the date at the top. Finally, put your pencil down and look up.'

Activity 2 – Instruction chain
In pairs, one pupil gives three simple instructions (e.g., 'Touch your head, clap twice, then turn around'). The other listens and performs. Swap roles. If you do not understand, ask politely: 'Please, can you repeat the second instruction?' (communication).

Digital corner: Listen to a recorded set of instructions on a phone or tablet (e.g., steps to draw a simple picture). Pause, repeat and follow. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.1

  1. Your teacher will read a short story. Answer: Who was the main person? What did they do first? How did the story end?
  2. Listen to the instruction: 'Stand up, push your chair in, walk to the front and count to five.' Perform it correctly.
  3. Write the polite question you would ask if you did not hear what your friend said.
  4. Give two reasons why listening is important at home and in school.

sessions.title: Greetings and Polite Conversation
indicators: Use appropriate time-of-day greetings and respond correctly
Use polite words: please, thank you, sorry, excuse me in conversations
Take turns to speak during group discussions
Role-play everyday situations requiring polite language (creativity, cultural identity)
Record a short greeting exchange and review for improvement (digital literacy)
Demonstrate respect through proper greetings in the community (personal development)
sessions.content:
Good Manners – Greetings and Magic Words

In Ghana, greeting is a sign of respect. It is important to greet everyone, especially elders, and to use polite words.

1. Time-of-Day Greetings

Morning: 'Good morning, Mummy.' 'Good morning, Mr. Tetteh.'
Afternoon: 'Good afternoon, Auntie Grace.' 'Good afternoon, sir.'
Evening: 'Good evening, Daddy.' 'Good evening, Nana.'

Always add the person's name or title. After greeting, ask 'How are you?' and listen to the reply.

Activity 1 – Greeting walk
Move around the classroom. Greet at least five classmates using the correct time-of-day greeting and a polite question. For example: 'Good afternoon, Akos. How are you today?' (communication, cultural identity).

2. Magic Words

  • Please – when you ask for something: 'Please, may I borrow your eraser?'
  • Thank you – when you receive help or a gift: 'Thank you for the pencil.'
  • Sorry – when you make a mistake or hurt someone: 'I am sorry I bumped into you.'
  • Excuse me – when you need to pass or get attention: 'Excuse me, teacher, may I ask a question?'

Activity 2 – Role-play situations
In pairs, act out these scenes: (a) You are buying bread at a shop. (b) You accidentally step on a friend's foot. (c) You want to borrow a sharpener. Use magic words. (creativity).

Digital corner: Record a short greeting conversation with a friend using a phone. Play it back and check: Did you use the correct greeting? Did you say please or thank you? (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.2

  1. Write the greeting you would use at 3 o'clock in the afternoon for your teacher.
  2. Write a sentence using each magic word: please, thank you, sorry, excuse me.
  3. Why is it important to take turns when speaking? Give one reason.
  4. Write a short dialogue between two friends meeting at the market in the morning. Use greetings and polite language.

sessions.title: Asking and Answering Questions
indicators: Ask questions using who, what, where, when, why and how
Answer questions in full sentences with appropriate details
Participate in question-and-answer sessions about pictures and stories
Work collaboratively to prepare and conduct a simple interview (collaboration, communication)
Use digital recording to practise asking and answering questions (digital literacy)
Recognise that asking good questions deepens understanding (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Curious Minds – Questions and Answers

Questions help us find out new things. We use special words to ask different kinds of questions.

1. Question Words

  • Who – asks about people: 'Who is your best friend?'
  • What – asks about things or actions: 'What did you eat for breakfast?'
  • Where – asks about places: 'Where do you live?'
  • When – asks about time: 'When is your birthday?'
  • Why – asks for a reason: 'Why do you go to school?'
  • How – asks about manner or condition: 'How do you come to school?' 'How are you feeling?'

Activity 1 – Question spinner
Make a spinner with the six question words. Spin and ask a partner a question using that word. Your partner must answer in a full sentence. For example, if you spin 'where', ask 'Where is your bag?' and the answer is 'My bag is under my desk.' (communication).

2. Answering in Full Sentences

Always answer with a complete sentence. Repeat part of the question in your answer.

Examples:
Question: 'Why do we wash our hands?'
Answer: 'We wash our hands to remove germs and stay healthy.'
Question: 'How did you come to school today?'
Answer: 'I walked to school with my sister.'

Activity 2 – Interview a classmate
In pairs, prepare five questions to learn about your partner's family, hobbies or favourite food. Take turns interviewing and then introduce your partner to the class using the information you gathered. (collaboration, communication).

Digital corner: Imagine you are a reporter. Use a phone to record a short interview with a family member. Listen to the recording and write down the answers you received. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.3

  1. Write a question for each question word: who, what, where, when, why, how.
  2. Answer this question in a full sentence: 'How do you help at home?'
  3. If someone asks 'Where is the headmaster's office?', write a polite answer in a full sentence.
  4. Create three questions you would ask a new pupil joining your class.

sessions.title: Storytelling – Retelling and Creating Stories
indicators: Retell a known story in the correct sequence using first, next, then, finally
Create and tell an original short story with a beginning, middle and end
Use gestures, facial expressions and voice changes to make a story interesting
Work in groups to develop and present a short story (creativity, collaboration)
Listen to and appreciate traditional Ananse stories (cultural identity)
Use digital recording to share stories with a wider audience (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
The Art of Storytelling

Stories are an important part of Ghanaian culture. Through stories, we learn lessons, entertain ourselves and keep our traditions alive.

1. Retelling a Story in Sequence

Every story has a beginning, a middle and an end. Use connecting words to show the order.

Example: Think of the story of 'The Tortoise and the Hare'.
Beginning: Tortoise and Hare decide to race.
Middle: Hare runs fast and sleeps; Tortoise walks slowly without stopping.
End: Tortoise wins the race.

Activity 1 – Story chain
Sit in a circle. The teacher starts a story with one sentence. Each pupil adds one sentence to continue the story. Try to keep the story logical and exciting. (collaboration).

2. Creating Original Stories

To make your own story, choose a main character, a setting and a problem. Decide what happens in the beginning, middle and end.

Activity 2 – Story mountain
Draw a mountain on paper. On the left side, write the beginning. At the top, write the middle (the problem). On the right side, write the end (the solution). Use your plan to tell your story to a partner. (creativity).

3. Telling with Expression

Good storytellers use a loud or soft voice, change their face to show feelings and use their hands to act out parts.

Activity 3 – Ananse storytelling
Listen to a traditional Ananse story told by your teacher or an elder. Practise retelling it with expression and gestures. Perform it for the class. (cultural identity).

Digital corner: Record your story using a phone or tablet. Play it for the class or share it with your parents. (digital literacy).

Exercise 1.4

  1. Retell a story you know in five sentences. Use first, next, then, after that and finally.
  2. Make up a story about a clever goat. Give it a title.
  3. What gestures would you use to show that a character is scared? Demonstrate.
  4. Why do we tell stories to children at home? Write one reason.

sessions.title: Phonics – Consonant Blends and Digraphs
indicators: Identify and pronounce common consonant blends (bl, cl, fl, gl, pl, sl, br, cr, dr, fr, gr, pr, tr, st, sp, sn, sm, sk, sw)
Identify and pronounce consonant digraphs (ch, sh, th, wh, ph)
Read and spell words containing blends and digraphs
Work in pairs to sort words by their initial sounds (collaboration)
Use digital phonics games to practise blends and digraphs (digital literacy)
Apply knowledge of blends to decode unfamiliar words while reading (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Blending Sounds – Two Letters Together

When two or three consonants appear together in a word, we blend their sounds. A blend means you can still hear each sound. A digraph means two letters make one new sound.

1. Consonant Blends

L-blends: bl (blue, black, blanket), cl (clap, clock, clean), fl (fly, flower, flat), gl (glass, glow, glue), pl (play, plate, plum), sl (sleep, slow, slide).

R-blends: br (brown, bring, bread), cr (cry, cross, crayon), dr (drum, drink, dress), fr (frog, fruit, friend), gr (green, grass, grow), pr (pray, present, proud), tr (tree, train, try).

S-blends: st (star, stop, stand), sp (spoon, speak, spider), sn (snake, snow, snack), sm (smile, small, smell), sk (skirt, skip, sky), sw (sweet, swim, swing).

Activity 1 – Blend hunt
Look around the classroom or in a storybook. Find five words that start with a blend and write them down. Share your list with a partner. (collaboration).

2. Consonant Digraphs

  • ch – chair, church, chicken (sound like 'ch' in 'chop')
  • sh – ship, shoe, fish (sound like 'sh' in 'she')
  • th – think, three, bath (voiceless); this, mother, brother (voiced)
  • wh – what, where, wheel (often pronounced /w/)
  • ph – phone, photo, alphabet (sounds like /f/)

Activity 2 – Digraph sort
Cut out words from old newspapers or magazines. Sort them into groups: ch, sh, th, wh, ph. Glue them onto a chart. (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a phonics app or website like Starfall or PhonicsPlay to listen to and match sounds. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.1

  1. Write two words for each blend: bl, cr, st, fl, gr, sp.
  2. Fill in the missing digraph: __air (ch), fi__ (sh), __umb (th), __oto (ph), __eel (wh).
  3. Read these words aloud: splash, threw, chapter, whisper.
  4. Write a sentence using at least two words with blends.

sessions.title: Phonics – Long and Short Vowels
indicators: Distinguish between short and long vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u)
Apply the silent-e rule to change short vowels to long vowels (e.g., cap to cape)
Read and spell words with vowel teams (ai, ea, oa, ee, oo)
Collaborate in a word-sorting activity to group words by vowel sound (collaboration)
Use digital interactive tools to practise vowel sounds (digital literacy)
Use phonics rules to decode new words independently (critical thinking, personal development)
sessions.content:
Vowel Sounds – Short and Long

Every word has at least one vowel. Vowels can say their sound (short) or their name (long). Knowing the difference helps you read and spell.

1. Short Vowel Sounds

  • a as in apple, cat, bag, fan
  • e as in egg, bed, ten, pen
  • i as in igloo, sit, pin, fish
  • o as in orange, hot, dog, pot
  • u as in umbrella, cup, sun, bus

Activity 1 – Vowel sound chart
Draw a chart with five columns, one for each short vowel. Cut out or draw pictures that contain each short vowel sound and paste them in the right column. (creativity).

2. Long Vowel Sounds and the Silent-e

When a word ends with an e that you do not say, it makes the vowel before it say its name.

Examples: cap becomes cape, pet becomes Pete, pin becomes pine, hop becomes hope, cut becomes cute.

Activity 2 – Magic e wand
Make a wand with a paper 'e'. Place it at the end of short vowel word cards (tap becomes tape, not becomes note). Read the new word aloud. (collaboration – work in pairs).

3. Vowel Teams

Two vowels together often make the first vowel say its name (long sound).

  • ai – rain, train, snail
  • ea – seat, read, beach
  • oa – boat, goat, road
  • ee – tree, three, sleep
  • oo – moon, spoon (long); book, foot (short)

Activity 3 – Vowel team bingo
Play bingo with words containing ai, ea, oa, ee, oo. The teacher calls a word, pupils find and mark it. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a free online phonics game like Teach Your Monster to Read to practise long and short vowels. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.2

  1. Sort these words into short and long vowel groups: bat, kite, rug, rope, bed, lake.
  2. Add silent-e to make a new word: tap becomes ___, fin becomes ___, rod becomes ___.
  3. Fill in the vowel team: r__n (ai/oa), b__t (oa/ee), tr__ (ee/ai).
  4. Write a sentence using two words with the ea team.

sessions.title: Reading Fluency and Expression
indicators: Read aloud with accuracy, appropriate speed and expression
Pay attention to punctuation marks (full stop, comma, question mark, exclamation mark) while reading
Read with natural phrasing, not word-by-word
Practise paired reading to build fluency (collaboration)
Record and listen to own reading to self-assess and improve (digital literacy, personal development)
Use expression to convey emotion and meaning (creativity)
sessions.content:
Reading Smoothly and with Feeling

Good readers read like they are talking. They do not stop after every word. They use the right voice for punctuation and show emotion.

1. Reading with Accuracy and Speed

First, make sure you know the words. Then try to read smoothly without stopping to sound out every letter. Practise the same passage several times until it flows.

Activity 1 – Timed repeated reading
Choose a short paragraph of about fifty words. Read it silently, then aloud. Time yourself. Read it again and see if you can get faster without making mistakes. (personal development).

2. Paying Attention to Punctuation

  • Full stop (.) – voice goes down and pause.
  • Comma (,) – brief pause.
  • Question mark (?) – voice goes up at the end.
  • Exclamation mark (!) – read with strong feeling.

Activity 2 – Punctuation detectives
Take a sentence and rewrite it with different punctuation. Read each version with the correct expression. For example, 'The dog is here.' vs. 'The dog is here!' vs. 'Is the dog here?'

3. Reading with Expression

Change your voice to show the character's feelings – happy, sad, scared, excited.

Activity 3 – Reader's theatre
In groups, choose a simple script or make one from a story. Practise reading your part with expression. Perform for the class. (creativity, collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a phone to record your reading. Listen. Do you sound like a robot or a storyteller? Try again to improve. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.3

  1. Read a page from your reading book aloud to a partner. Ask your partner to tell you two things you did well and one thing to improve.
  2. Copy this sentence and add the correct punctuation: 'help there is a snake'
  3. How should your voice sound when you read a question?
  4. Write a short dialogue between two characters and read it with expression.

sessions.title: Comprehension – Main Idea and Details
indicators: Identify the main idea of a short passage
Find supporting details that tell more about the main idea
Answer literal and inferential questions from a text
Work in groups to discuss and justify answers (collaboration, critical thinking)
Use digital reading comprehension apps to practise (digital literacy)
Apply comprehension strategies to real-life information (personal development)
sessions.content:
Understanding What We Read

Reading is not just saying words; it is understanding the message. The main idea is what the whole passage is mostly about. The details give more information.

1. Finding the Main Idea

Ask: 'What is the one big thing the writer wants me to know?' The main idea is often found in the first or last sentence.

Example: 'Elephants are the largest land animals. They have long trunks, big ears and thick grey skin. They use their trunks to pick up food, drink water and even greet each other.'
Main idea: Elephants are large animals with special body parts.
Details: long trunks, big ears, thick grey skin; trunks used for food, water, greeting.

Activity 1 – Main idea bags
Put small objects related to one topic in a bag (e.g., pencil, eraser, sharpener – 'school supplies'). Pupils guess the main idea. (creativity, collaboration).

2. Literal and Inferential Questions

Literal questions have answers right there in the text. Inferential questions require you to think and use clues.

Example: 'Kofi came to school wearing a heavy coat and carrying an umbrella. His shoes were wet.'
Literal: What was Kofi carrying? (umbrella)
Inferential: What was the weather like? (It was raining, because wet shoes and umbrella.)

Activity 2 – Question sort
After reading a short story, write two literal and two inferential questions on cards. Swap with a partner and answer. (critical thinking).

Digital corner: Use a reading app like ReadTheory that asks main idea questions and gives feedback. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.4

  1. Read the passage: 'Kwame loves football. He plays every day after school. He wants to be a professional player when he grows up.' What is the main idea?
  2. List two details from the passage.
  3. Literal: What does Kwame do after school?
  4. Inferential: How do you think Kwame feels about football? Why?
  5. Write a short paragraph about your favourite food. Underline the main idea.

sessions.title: Comprehension – Sequencing Events
indicators: Identify the order of events in a story
Use signal words: first, next, then, after that, finally
Retell a story in the correct sequence
Collaborate to arrange jumbled sentences into the right order (collaboration)
Use digital story-mapping tools to organise events (digital literacy)
Apply sequencing to follow instructions in real-life tasks (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
What Happened When? – Sequencing Events

Things happen in a certain order. Knowing the sequence helps you understand a story and follow instructions.

1. Signal Words for Sequence

Writers use words to show time order: first, next, then, after that, later, finally.

Example: 'First, Abena woke up. Next, she brushed her teeth. Then she ate her breakfast. After that, she put on her uniform. Finally, she walked to school.'

Activity 1 – Sequence dance
Create a simple dance routine with four moves. Describe it using first, next, then, finally. Perform it. (creativity).

2. Arranging Events in Order

When you read a story, think about what happened at the beginning, middle and end.

Activity 2 – Sentence sorting
In groups, the teacher gives you strips of paper with sentences from a story mixed up. Work together to put them in the right order. Glue onto a chart. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a drawing app to create a simple comic strip of three or four pictures showing a sequence of events. Add captions. (digital literacy).

3. Following Real-Life Sequence

We use sequencing to follow recipes, give directions or explain how to do something.

Activity 3 – How-to guide
Write a how-to guide for something you know: how to plant a seed, how to wash your hands properly, how to play ampe. Use sequence words.

Exercise 2.5

  1. Put these in order using words: 'Ama put the cake in the oven. She mixed flour and sugar. She ate the cake. She baked it for thirty minutes.'
  2. Read a short story your teacher gives you. Write what happened first, next, then, finally.
  3. Write instructions for making your favourite drink. Use sequencing words.
  4. Why is it important to do things in the right order? Give an example.

sessions.title: Vocabulary Building – Synonyms and Antonyms
indicators: Identify and use synonyms (words with similar meanings)
Identify and use antonyms (words with opposite meanings)
Use a simple thesaurus or word bank to find alternative words
Work in pairs to play synonym-antonym matching games (collaboration)
Use digital word tools like a children's online dictionary to expand vocabulary (digital literacy)
Use a variety of words to make speech and writing more interesting (creativity)
sessions.content:
Words That Mean the Same or Opposite

Using different words makes your speaking and writing exciting. Synonyms are words with the same or nearly the same meaning. Antonyms are words with opposite meanings.

1. Synonyms

Examples: big – large, small – tiny, happy – glad, fast – quick, smart – clever, beautiful – pretty, sad – unhappy.

Activity 1 – Synonym circle
In groups, stand in a circle. The teacher says a word like 'big'. The next person says a synonym like 'large'. Go around until you run out. (collaboration).

2. Antonyms

Examples: hot – cold, tall – short, dry – wet, up – down, day – night, open – close, rich – poor, fast – slow.

Activity 2 – Antonym match
Make cards with words and their antonyms. Shuffle, turn them face down and play a matching memory game. (collaboration).

3. Using Synonyms and Antonyms in Writing

Instead of saying 'The dog was big', you can say 'The dog was enormous' or 'The dog was gigantic'. Instead of 'The girl was happy but the boy was sad', you can use 'The girl was joyful but the boy was miserable'.

Activity 3 – Sentence improvement
Rewrite these sentences with more interesting words: 'The man was old. He walked slowly. The house was big.' (creativity).

Digital corner: Visit a child-friendly online thesaurus like Wordsmyth. Search for a word and find its synonym and antonym. (digital literacy).

Exercise 2.6

  1. Write a synonym for: happy, angry, pretty, quiet, start.
  2. Write an antonym for: hard, light, full, love, give.
  3. Fill in the blanks with a synonym of the word in brackets: The cake was ________ (delicious). The room was ________ (tidy).
  4. Write two sentences: one using a pair of synonyms, one using a pair of antonyms.

sessions.title: Penmanship – Letter Formation and Joined Writing
indicators: Form letters correctly with consistent size and spacing
Join letters to write simple words legibly in cursive or joined manuscript
Write sentences neatly and clearly
Practise writing drills to improve handwriting (personal development)
Peer-assess handwriting for legibility (collaboration)
Use digital handwriting practice apps if available (digital literacy)
sessions.content:
Beautiful Handwriting – Clear and Neat

Good handwriting makes your work easy to read. In Basic 2, we continue to practise correct letter formation and begin joining letters.

1. Letter Formation and Spacing

Each letter has a correct shape and size. Keep letters sitting on the line. Leave a small finger space between words.

Activity 1 – Warm-up patterns
Draw loops, zig-zags and curves in the air, then on paper. This relaxes your hand. (personal development).

2. Joining Letters

Start joining simple letters. Practice joins like a to n, c to a, i to n.

Example: Write 'an, can, in, and, cat, dog, sun' without lifting your pencil.

Activity 2 – Copy and join
Copy a short sentence in your best joined writing: 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' Swap books with a partner and circle the neatest word. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a stylus on a tablet or a handwriting app to trace and write letters. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.1

  1. Write the lower-case alphabet in joined letters.
  2. Copy the sentence: 'Ghana is a beautiful country.' three times, trying to improve each time.
  3. What are three things you can do to make your handwriting better?

sessions.title: Spelling – High-Frequency Words and Rules
indicators: Spell common high-frequency words correctly (e.g., because, friend, school, beautiful)
Apply simple spelling rules (doubling consonants, changing y to i, dropping silent e)
Use the look, say, cover, write, check method to learn spellings
Work in pairs to test each other on spelling words (collaboration)
Use digital spelling games to practise (digital literacy)
Develop a personal spelling journal (personal development)
sessions.content:
Spelling Right – Common Words and Rules

Spelling correctly helps people understand your writing. You must learn many words by heart and know a few rules.

1. High-Frequency Words

These words appear often and you should know them: because, friend, school, beautiful, people, teacher, window, before, after, always, never, through, thought, although.

Activity 1 – Look, Say, Cover, Write, Check
1. Look at the word. 2. Say it aloud. 3. Cover it. 4. Write it from memory. 5. Check if it is correct. Do this five times for each new word.

2. Spelling Rules

  • Doubling consonants: In short vowel words ending in one consonant, double before adding -ed or -ing (hop becomes hopped, run becomes running).
  • Changing y to i: If a word ends in y after a consonant, change y to i before adding -es or -ed (cry becomes cries, carry becomes carried). But keep the y before -ing (crying, carrying).
  • Drop silent e: Before adding -ing or -ed, drop the silent e (make becomes making, hope becomes hoped).

Activity 2 – Spelling partner test
Work with a partner. Take turns dictating five words from the high-frequency list. Mark each other's work. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use a spelling app or website like Spelling City to enter your word list and play games. (digital literacy).

Activity 3 – My spelling journal
Keep a small notebook. Every time you find a word difficult to spell, write it in your journal and practise it. (personal development).

Exercise 3.2

  1. Write these words correctly: frend, becos, butiful, skool.
  2. Apply the rule: add -ing to: run, swim, make, write.
  3. Add -ed to: carry, cry, bake, stop.
  4. Write a sentence using three high-frequency words.

sessions.title: Sentence Construction – Capital Letters and Full Stops
indicators: Construct simple sentences with correct word order
Begin every sentence with a capital letter
End sentences with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark
Work in groups to build sentences from jumbled words (collaboration)
Use digital word-processing tools to type sentences and check capitals (digital literacy)
Proofread own and others' writing for sentence errors (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Building Complete Sentences

A sentence is a group of words that tells a complete idea. Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with an end mark.

1. What Makes a Sentence?

A sentence must have a subject (who or what) and a verb (action or state of being).

Example: 'The girl runs.' Subject: The girl; verb: runs. This is a complete sentence. 'The girl' alone is not a sentence.

Activity 1 – Sentence or not?
Hold up a card: 'The big brown dog.' (Not a sentence – no verb). 'The big brown dog barked loudly.' (Yes). Pupils give thumbs up or down. (critical thinking).

2. Capital Letters

Always use a capital letter for:

  • The first word of a sentence.
  • Names of people, places, days and months (Kofi, Ghana, Monday, July).
  • The word I.

Activity 2 – Jumbled sentences
In groups, arrange word cards to make a correct sentence. Remember the capital letter and full stop. (collaboration).

3. End Marks

  • Full stop (.) – for statements and commands.
  • Question mark (?) – for questions.
  • Exclamation mark (!) – for strong feelings.

Activity 3 – Sentence doctor
Read sentences with mistakes. Fix them: 'the dog is brown' becomes 'The dog is brown.' 'where is the ball' becomes 'Where is the ball?' (critical thinking).

Digital corner: Type your sentences on a computer or tablet. Notice how the program automatically capitalises the first letter. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.3

  1. Rewrite correctly: 'my friend ama lives in tamale'
  2. Add capital letters and end marks: 'can you see the rainbow'
  3. Write three sentences about your school. Check capitals and end marks.
  4. Change the statement to a question: 'He is coming.'

sessions.title: Writing a Paragraph – Topic Sentence and Supporting Details
indicators: Write a topic sentence that states the main idea
Add at least three supporting detail sentences
Use appropriate linking words to connect ideas
Collaborate to build a paragraph from a mind map (collaboration)
Use digital graphic organisers to plan a paragraph (digital literacy)
Evaluate own paragraph for unity and coherence (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Putting Ideas Together – The Paragraph

A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea. It has a topic sentence (what the paragraph is about) and supporting sentences (details).

1. The Topic Sentence

Usually the first sentence tells the main idea.

Example: 'My mother is a very kind person.' This tells us the paragraph will be about the mother's kindness.

Activity 1 – Spot the topic
Read a short paragraph and underline the topic sentence. (critical thinking).

2. Supporting Details

Add sentences that explain or prove the topic sentence.

Example: 'My mother is a very kind person. She helps our neighbours when they are sick. She gives food to the poor. She always listens to my problems and comforts me.'

Activity 2 – Mind map to paragraph
In pairs, make a mind map about 'My Best Friend'. In the centre, write the name. Around it, add words like: kind, funny, likes football, helps me. Then use the mind map to write a paragraph with a topic sentence and three details. (collaboration, creativity).

3. Linking Words

Use words like also, and, additionally, for example, because to connect ideas smoothly.

Digital corner: Use a computer or tablet to open a graphic organiser template from Canva or Google Docs. Plan your paragraph. (digital literacy).

Exercise 3.4

  1. Write a topic sentence about your favourite food.
  2. Add three supporting sentences to complete the paragraph.
  3. Underline the topic sentence and circle the linking words in your paragraph.
  4. Read your partner's paragraph. Does every sentence stick to the main idea? Suggest one improvement.

sessions.title: Creative Writing – Describing People and Places
indicators: Use descriptive words (adjectives) to describe people, places and things
Write a short descriptive paragraph with sensory details (sight, sound, smell, touch)
Organise ideas before writing using a simple plan
Share writing with peers and give positive feedback (collaboration, communication)
Use digital tools to add pictures to descriptions (digital literacy, creativity)
Reflect on how description helps the reader imagine (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Painting with Words – Descriptions

Good writers use words that help you see, hear, smell, taste and feel things. This is called descriptive writing.

1. Using Adjectives for Description

Adjectives tell us more about nouns.

Examples: a tall, green tree; a noisy, crowded market; a kind, gentle grandmother.

Activity 1 – Describe an object
Bring an object like a fruit or a toy. Write five adjectives to describe it. Then use them in sentences.

2. Sensory Details

Describe what you see, hear, smell, taste and touch.

Example: 'The market was busy. I saw colourful cloths hanging everywhere. I heard women calling out prices. I smelled fresh bread and smoked fish. I felt the rough texture of the baskets.'

Activity 2 – Sensory walk
Take a mental walk to a familiar place like the school garden. Write one sentence for each sense. (creativity).

3. Writing a Descriptive Paragraph

Plan first: Who or what are you describing? What are the most important details?

Activity 3 – My favourite person
Write a descriptive paragraph about a person you love. Describe how they look, what their voice sounds like and how they make you feel. Share with a partner. (collaboration, communication).

Digital corner: Type your description on a computer. Insert a picture of the place or person or draw one using a drawing app. (digital literacy, creativity).

Exercise 3.5

  1. Write five adjectives that describe your classroom.
  2. Describe the sound of rain on a roof in one sentence.
  3. Write a paragraph describing your school compound. Include at least three sensory details.
  4. Read your paragraph to a friend. Ask: 'What picture did you see in your mind?'

sessions.title: Nouns – Common, Proper, Singular and Plural
indicators: Distinguish between common and proper nouns
Form regular plural nouns by adding -s or -es
Identify and use irregular plurals (child/children, foot/feet)
Work collaboratively to sort nouns into categories (collaboration)
Use digital interactive noun games (digital literacy)
Apply correct noun forms in own writing (personal development)
sessions.content:
Naming Words – Nouns

A noun names a person, place, thing or idea.

1. Common vs Proper Nouns

Common nouns are general names: girl, city, day.
Proper nouns are specific names and begin with a capital letter: Akua, Accra, Monday.

Activity 1 – Noun sort
Sort a list of words into common and proper nouns. (collaboration).

2. Singular and Plural Nouns

Singular means one, plural means more than one.

  • Most nouns: add -s (cat becomes cats).
  • Nouns ending in s, sh, ch, x, z: add -es (box becomes boxes, church becomes churches).
  • Nouns ending in consonant + y: change y to i and add -es (baby becomes babies).
  • Irregular plurals: man becomes men, woman becomes women, child becomes children, tooth becomes teeth, foot becomes feet, mouse becomes mice, sheep remains sheep.

Activity 2 – Plural match
Match singular cards to plural cards. Play a memory game. (collaboration).

Digital corner: Use an online plural noun game to practise. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.1

  1. Circle the proper nouns: table, Kofi, Ghana, school, River Volta.
  2. Write the plural: bus, watch, fly, potato, deer, child.
  3. Fill in: There are three ______ (woman) and two ______ (man) in the room.
  4. Write two sentences, each with a singular and plural noun.

sessions.title: Verbs – Simple Present and Past Tense
indicators: Identify verbs as action words
Use simple present tense for habits and facts
Form simple past tense by adding -ed (regular) and using irregular forms
Work in pairs to act out verbs and guess tense (collaboration)
Use digital verb-tense quizzes for practice (digital literacy)
Use correct tense when writing about past events (personal development)
sessions.content:
Action Words – Verbs and Time

A verb shows action or a state of being. The form of the verb changes to show when the action happens.

1. Simple Present Tense

Used for habits, routines and facts. For third person singular (he, she, it), add -s or -es to the verb.

Examples: I eat rice every day. She eats rice every day. We play football on Saturdays.

Activity 1 – Daily routine
Write five sentences about what you do every morning. Underline the present tense verbs.

2. Simple Past Tense

Shows an action that happened before now.

  • Regular verbs: add -ed (play becomes played, walk becomes walked). If ends in e, just add -d (dance becomes danced).
  • Irregular verbs: change completely (go becomes went, eat becomes ate, see becomes saw, run becomes ran, do becomes did, have becomes had, come became came).

Activity 2 – Verb charades
A pupil picks a verb card and acts it out. Others guess the verb and say a sentence in the past tense. (collaboration, creativity).

Digital corner: Use an online verb tense quiz to practise past tense forms. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.2

  1. Complete with present tense: He ____ (go) to school every day.
  2. Change to past tense: She talks. She ____. They run. They ____.
  3. Write the past tense of: buy, see, eat, make, do.
  4. Write three sentences about what you did last Saturday.

sessions.title: Pronouns – Personal Pronouns
indicators: Identify personal pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they)
Use pronouns correctly to replace nouns in sentences
Ensure pronoun agrees with its antecedent
Work in pairs to replace nouns with pronouns in stories (collaboration)
Use digital pronoun exercises to reinforce learning (digital literacy)
Avoid unnecessary repetition in writing by using pronouns (creativity)
sessions.content:
Stand-in Words – Pronouns

A pronoun is a word that takes the place of a noun. It stops us from repeating the same noun again and again.

1. Personal Pronouns

  • I – the person speaking
  • You – the person being spoken to
  • He – a male person
  • She – a female person
  • It – a thing or animal
  • We – a group including the speaker
  • They – a group of people or things

Example: 'Kofi is tall. Kofi likes to read. Kofi has a book.' becomes 'Kofi is tall. He likes to read. He has a book.'

Activity 1 – Pronoun swap
Take a short paragraph that overuses a name. Replace the repeated nouns with pronouns. Read aloud to see if it still makes sense. (collaboration).

2. Pronoun Agreement

The pronoun must match the noun it replaces in number and gender: 'The girls are playing. They are happy.' (Not 'She is happy.')

Activity 2 – Story editing
Write a short story about two children. Use he, she and they correctly. Exchange with a partner and check pronoun use. (collaboration, critical thinking).

Digital corner: Use a grammar app to play pronoun matching games. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.3

  1. Rewrite using pronouns: 'Ama and I went to the market. Ama and I bought oranges. The oranges were sweet.'
  2. Fill in: 'My brother is late. ____ missed the bus.'
  3. Circle the pronoun: 'They are going to the park.'
  4. Write two sentences about your teacher using she or he.

sessions.title: Adjectives – Describing Words
indicators: Identify adjectives that describe colour, size, shape, number and feeling
Use adjectives before nouns and after verbs (e.g., the red ball; the ball is red)
Write sentences using interesting adjectives
Collaborate to brainstorm adjectives for a given picture (collaboration)
Use digital thesaurus to find better adjectives (digital literacy)
Enhance own stories by adding vivid adjectives (creativity)
sessions.content:
Making Writing Colourful – Adjectives

Adjectives describe nouns. They tell us what kind, how many and which one.

1. Types of Adjectives

  • Colour: red, blue, golden, dark
  • Size: big, tiny, long, short
  • Shape: round, square, flat
  • Number: three, many, few
  • Feeling: happy, sad, excited, angry

Activity 1 – Picture prompts
Show a picture of a busy market. In groups, list as many adjectives as you can to describe what you see. Compare lists. (collaboration, creativity).

2. Position of Adjectives

Adjectives usually come before the noun: 'a beautiful flower'. They can also come after the verb to be: 'The flower is beautiful.'

Activity 2 – Adjective detectives
Read a paragraph. Circle all adjectives. Discuss how they help you picture the scene.

3. Using Stronger Adjectives

Instead of 'big', use 'enormous'. Instead of 'good', use 'fantastic'.

Activity 3 – Adjective upgrade
Rewrite boring sentences with better adjectives: 'The man was old. The food was nice. The room was dirty.' (creativity).

Digital corner: Use an online children's thesaurus to find better adjectives. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.4

  1. Add an adjective: The ____ dog barked. I saw a ____ rainbow.
  2. Underline the adjectives: The little, brown bird sang a sweet song.
  3. Write three sentences describing your best friend's appearance using adjectives.
  4. Change the adjective to make the sentence more interesting: 'The cake was good.'

sessions.title: Prepositions of Place – In, On, Under, Behind, Next to, In front of
indicators: Identify prepositions of place: in, on, under, behind, between, next to, in front of
Use prepositions to describe the position of objects
Construct sentences that include prepositional phrases
Work collaboratively to give and follow directions using prepositions (collaboration)
Use digital mapping or drawing tools to create a room plan and describe positions (digital literacy)
Apply knowledge of prepositions to understand instructions in real life (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Where Is It? – Prepositions

Prepositions of place tell us where something is. They show the relationship between things.

1. Common Prepositions of Place

  • in – inside: The book is in the bag.
  • on – touching the surface: The cup is on the table.
  • under – below: The cat is under the chair.
  • behind – at the back of: The tree is behind the house.
  • between – in the middle of two things: She sits between Kofi and Ama.
  • next to – beside: The shop is next to the church.
  • in front of – before: The car is in front of the gate.

Activity 1 – Classroom treasure hunt
Follow oral instructions using prepositions: 'Put your pencil on your head. Now put it under your chair. Now put it between your two hands.' (collaboration).

2. Describing Positions

Look around and describe where things are using prepositions.

Activity 2 – Draw and describe
Draw a simple picture of your bedroom. Write five sentences describing where things are. Use at least three different prepositions. Share with a partner. (creativity, communication).

Digital corner: Use a simple drawing app to create a room layout. Label items with prepositions. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.5

  1. Fill in: The ball is ____ the box (inside). The clock is ____ the wall (on).
  2. Choose the correct preposition: The dog is sleeping (in, under) the table.
  3. Write a sentence using between.
  4. Describe the position of your exercise book right now using a preposition.

sessions.title: Sentence Types – Statements, Questions, Commands
indicators: Distinguish between statements, questions and commands
Write examples of each sentence type with correct punctuation
Change a statement into a question and vice versa
Work in groups to create role-plays demonstrating different sentence types (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital flashcard apps to practise identifying sentence types (digital literacy)
Apply knowledge of sentence types in everyday communication (personal development)
sessions.content:
Different Kinds of Sentences

We use different types of sentences for different purposes. They end with different punctuation.

1. Statements (Declarative)

A statement gives information. It ends with a full stop.
Example: The sun is hot. I like reading.

2. Questions (Interrogative)

A question asks something. It ends with a question mark.
Example: Where is your bag? Do you like mangoes?

3. Commands (Imperative)

A command tells someone to do something. It can end with a full stop or an exclamation mark if strong.
Example: Close the door. Stop shouting!

Activity 1 – Sentence sort
Give each group a set of sentence cards. Sort them into Statements, Questions, Commands. Check with another group. (collaboration, critical thinking).

Activity 2 – Role-play shopping
In pairs, act out a market scene. Use all three sentence types: 'How much is this cloth?' (question), 'It is five cedis.' (statement), 'Give me two yards, please.' (command). (creativity, cultural identity).

Digital corner: Use a quiz app like Quizlet to flash sentences and tap which type they are. (digital literacy).

Exercise 4.6

  1. Write what type each sentence is: (a) What a beautiful day! (b) The cat is sleeping. (c) Sit down.
  2. Change to a question: 'You are hungry.'
  3. Write a command you might hear in the classroom.
  4. Write one statement, one question and one command about your school.

sessions.title: Appreciating Poems and Rhymes
indicators: Recite simple poems and rhymes with rhythm and expression
Identify rhyming words in a poem
Identify the theme or message of a poem
Work in groups to create an original short poem or rhyme (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital recording to present a poem performance (digital literacy)
Appreciate Ghanaian traditional rhymes and poems (cultural identity)
sessions.content:
The Music of Words – Poems and Rhymes

Poems use words in a special way. They often have rhyme (words that end with the same sound) and rhythm (a beat).

1. Rhyming Words

Example: 'I have a cat, who wears a hat, he is so fat, and that is that.' Rhyming words: cat, hat, fat, that.

Activity 1 – Rhyme time
Teacher says a word, you say a rhyme: 'day' – 'say'; 'night' – 'light'; 'fun' – 'run'. Make a class rhyme bank. (collaboration).

2. Reciting with Expression

Poems should be read with feeling and a clear voice.

Activity 2 – Class poetry recital
Learn a short traditional Ghanaian rhyme or one from your textbook. Practise in groups, add claps or drumming. Perform for the class. (creativity, cultural identity).

3. The Message of a Poem

Ask: What is the poem about? What does the poet want us to learn or feel?

Activity 3 – Write a couplet
A couplet is two lines that rhyme. Write one about a friend, animal or nature. Share it aloud. (creativity).

Digital corner: Record your poem recital using a phone. Listen and improve your expression. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.1

  1. Write three words that rhyme with 'tree'.
  2. Recite a short poem you know. What is its message?
  3. Create a four-line poem about the rain. Make lines two and four rhyme.
  4. Why do we enjoy listening to poems and songs?

sessions.title: Listening to and Retelling Folk Tales
indicators: Listen attentively to a folk tale and recall key events
Identify the main character, problem and solution
Retell the folk tale in own words, maintaining the correct sequence
Work in groups to dramatise a folk tale (creativity, collaboration)
Discuss the moral lesson of the story (critical thinking, personal development)
Appreciate the role of folk tales in preserving Ghanaian culture (cultural identity)
sessions.content:
Stories of Our Elders – Folk Tales

Folk tales are stories passed down from our ancestors. They often feature animals that talk and teach us important lessons.

1. Elements of a Folk Tale

Every tale has characters, a setting, a problem (conflict) and a solution (how it ends).

Example: Ananse the spider often tricks others but sometimes learns a lesson.

Activity 1 – Story map
Listen to a folk tale told by your teacher or an elder. Draw a story map: characters, setting, problem, solution. (critical thinking).

2. Retelling the Story

Use the story map to retell the tale in your own words. Remember the sequence and use connecting words.

Activity 2 – Group dramatisation
In groups, choose a short folk tale. Assign roles and act it out with simple costumes or props. (creativity, collaboration).

3. The Moral Lesson

Folk tales teach us values: honesty, hard work, kindness, wisdom. After each tale ask: 'What did we learn?'

Activity 3 – Lesson discussion
Discuss: 'Why do you think our grandparents told us these stories? What lesson do you still remember from a story?' (cultural identity, personal development).

Digital corner: Search for an animated Ananse story online (with teacher guidance). Watch and compare with the told version. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.2

  1. Name one character from a folk tale you know. Was he or she clever or foolish?
  2. Write three sentences retelling the beginning of a folk tale you have heard.
  3. What was the problem in the story? How was it solved?
  4. What lesson did you learn from the story?

sessions.title: Describing Characters in Stories
indicators: Identify and list character traits (e.g., brave, kind, greedy, clever)
Use evidence from the story to support descriptions
Compare two characters from the same story
Collaborate to create a character portrait using words and pictures (creativity, collaboration)
Use digital drawing or writing tools to create a character profile (digital literacy)
Reflect on how characters' actions affect the story (critical thinking)
sessions.content:
Who Is in the Story? – Characters

Characters are the people or animals in a story. We learn about them by what they say, do and think.

1. Character Traits

Traits describe what kind of person a character is.
Examples: kind, mean, brave, fearful, honest, greedy, generous, curious, lazy, hard-working.

Activity 1 – Trait detective
Read a short story. List the main character's traits and write one action that proves each trait. (e.g., 'Kofi is brave because he entered the dark forest alone.') (critical thinking).

2. Comparing Characters

Find how two characters are alike and different.

Example: In 'The Lion and the Mouse', the lion is powerful but proud; the mouse is small but clever. Both are kind in the end.

Activity 2 – Venn diagram
Draw two overlapping circles. Label one with Character A, one with Character B. Write traits unique to each in the outer parts, and shared traits in the middle. (collaboration).

3. Creating a Character Portrait

Draw the character and write a description around it: name, traits, what they like, what they fear, a quote from the story.

Activity 3 – Wanted poster
Create a 'Wanted' poster for a story character (good or bad). Include a picture, name, traits and why they are wanted (for help or for mischief). (creativity).

Digital corner: Use a word processing or drawing app to make your character poster. Add colour and text boxes. (digital literacy).

Exercise 5.3

  1. Name the main character of a story you read recently. List three traits.
  2. Write one sentence to prove that the character has one of those traits.
  3. Compare yourself to a story character. How are you alike? How are you different?
  4. Draw your favourite character and write a caption describing them.
